correctness.rationale: Arbitrary antiderivative tests in \(x\), \(y\), and \(z\) give the three conditional laws. Conditional orthogonality yields the two variance defects. Stationarity of the squared fast residual gives \(\mathbb E[\dot x\dot y]=\mathbb E[h^{\prime}(x)\dot x^2]\), while stationarity of \(\dot y^2/2\) and \(y^2/2\) gives \(\mathbb E[\dot x\dot y]=\mathbb E[\dot y^2]\). The Lipschitz breakpoint issue is harmless because invariant measures have zero \(\dot x^2\)-weighted mass on transversal breakplanes. The sector identity follows from \(\mathbb E[y\mid z]=0\), stationarity of \(y^2/2\), and \(\mathbb E[y\mid x]=h(x)\). Zero coordinate-speed energy is rigorously classified as equilibrium support. The classical thresholds are exact rational consequences verified by the packaged checker.

value.rationale: The negative inner slope and positive outer slope are the defining circuit geometry behind Chua’s double scroll. The accepted theorem converts that geometry into an exact stationary budget: the \(y\)-speed energy equals the \(x\)-speed energy weighted by the instantaneous branch slope. This forces every genuinely recurrent stationary state to dynamically use the positive-slope outer branches and, together with the sector-energy identity, to reach beyond the nonzero equilibrium voltage magnitude. At the classical slopes it gives two concrete diagnostics—positive mass beyond \(|x|=3/2\) and a strict one-third lower bound on outer-branch \(x\)-speed energy—that apply to every compact periodic or chaotic stationary state, not just one simulated attractor.
